    17	
    18	# Toward Functional and Non-Functional Evaluation of Application-Level Code Generation
    19	
    20	- Authors: Pan, Ruwei; Zhang, Yakun; Liang, Qingyuan; Zhu, Yueheng; Liu, Chao; Zhang, Lu; Zhang, Hongyu
    21	- Year / venue: 2026, arXiv (preprint, not peer-reviewed; the PDF carries an unfilled ACM "Conference'17" template header)
    22	- DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2602.03462 · URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.03462
    23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
    24	
    25	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
    26	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
    27	
    28	## 1. Research objective
    29	- [A] Test whether current LLMs can generate *application-level* repositories (runnable, multi-file, with dependencies, executable end to end) that satisfy both functional correctness and non-functional quality attributes. The authors argue that function-, contest-, repo-completion- and feature-level benchmarks do not test this (p. 1).
    30	- [A] Introduce RAL-Bench (Real-World Application-Level Code Generation Bench): a benchmark and evaluation framework that derives a natural-language requirement from a real reference project and tests generated repositories with reference-validated black-box system tests (p. 1).
    31	
    32	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
    33	- [V] RQ1: how well current LLMs perform at application-level generation; RQ2: where they fail; RQ3: what it costs; RQ4: whether mainstream generation strategies help (p. 5).
    34	- No formal hypotheses stated.
    35	
    36	## 3. Methodology
    37	- Research design: [V] Benchmark construction, then a controlled, single-turn, zero-shot comparison of 16 LLMs, plus a manual failure taxonomy, a cost analysis, a single-model strategy ablation, and prompt-sensitivity and metric-robustness checks (p. 4; p. 5; p. 9).
    38	- Approach / model / intervention: [V] Each LLM receives (a) a short NL requirement drafted from the reference project's README, public API, usage examples and source code, then manually edited to remove implementation details, file-layout hints and project-specific names, and (b) the reference repository's expected module/package surface (an "interface specification"). It outputs the whole repository in one pass (p. 2; p. 4; p. 5). [V] For GPT-5.2 on Stegano, adding the interface specification raised the functional score from 0.1667 to 0.6667, attributed to fewer entry-point/module-path mismatches (p. 4).
    39	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] 11 "standard" and 5 "thinking" LLMs are compared with each other. There is no non-LLM or human baseline; the reference repository is used only as a normalisation anchor for non-functional scores (p. 4; p. 5). [V] RQ4 compares the GPT-5.2 baseline with three one-shot strategies: S1 feedback-driven self-repair, S2 automated environment repair, S3 planning-driven generation (p. 8).
    40	- [I] Relation to our topic: the "reference" is a real application, and generated code is judged on tests that pass on that reference. This is close to rebuilding an existing app from its specification. However, the model never sees or runs the reference. It gets a distilled text requirement plus the API surface, so this is spec-to-app generation, not black-box behavioural reverse engineering.
    41	
    42	## 4. Dataset and sample
    43	- Data source(s): [V] 38 actively maintained Python GitHub projects (e.g. tabulate, click, requests, celery, mitmproxy, sqlmap), each pinned to a commit SHA and grouped into seven scenarios (Tooling, Data, Web, Security, Automation, Observability, Content). Sizes range from 1 to 242 files and 0.3k to 109.5k LoC (p. 2).
    44	- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] 38 tasks with "more than 450 evaluation points" (p. 2). [V] Functional tests per task: mean 11.03, median 11.5, min 10, max 19. Executable suites per task: mean 17.66 (p. 5). [V] 16 LLMs, 3 runs each (p. 5). [V] The failure analysis covers 446 generated repositories and more than 4,500 test execution logs (p. 7).
    45	- Sampling / selection method: [V] Three criteria: clearly documented functionality, stable public interfaces suitable for end-to-end tests, and active real-world use. Average popularity is above 1,000 stars, and repositories already used in public code-generation benchmarks are excluded (p. 2). How the 38 were picked from the candidate pool: not reported.
    46	- Data availability (public? link?): [A] All scripts and data are released at github.com/Wwstarry/RAL-Bench (p. 11). The AHP derivation is said to be in an "anonymous repository" (p. 4).
    47	
    48	## 5. Experimental setup
    49	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] Zero-shot, each model's default prompt template, the whole repository generated in one pass within context limits, three repeats averaged (p. 5). [A] The abstract says "greedy decoding" (p. 1). The setup section does not restate temperature or decoding parameters (not reported in Section 3.1). [V] Tests are pytest suites run against the generated repository; the functional score is the pass ratio (p. 3; p. 4). [V] Non-functional pipeline (p. 3; p. 4):
    50	  - maintainability: lower-bound Maintainability Index (MI) from static analysis;
    51	  - security: number of high-risk static-analysis findings;
    52	  - robustness: pass rate on an invalid/boundary-input suite;
    53	  - efficiency: runtime of an efficiency suite;
    54	  - resource: average RSS memory and CPU during a resource suite.
    55	  
    56	  Each is normalised against the reference repository and capped at 1. The static-analysis tools are not named in the text; Fig. 3 shows only "mi_min" and "high_risk_count" (p. 4). [V] Aggregate NF = 0.36 M + 0.24 S + 0.16 Rb + 0.12 E + 0.12 Ru. The weights come from AHP (analytic hierarchy process, a method that turns pairwise importance judgements into weights) applied to an ordering taken from Botchway et al.; consistency ratio 0.030 (p. 4).
    57	- [V] Rerun stability: the full pipeline was rerun 5 times for GPT-5.2, Gemini-3-Pro-Preview and Claude-4.5-Sonnet (p. 6; p. 7).
    58	- [V] Cost: provider token pricing, generation only, excluding test execution (p. 8).
    59	- Code availability: [A] public GitHub repository (p. 11).
    60	
    61	## 6. Evaluation metrics
    62	- Functional score: pass rate of reference-validated black-box functional tests. Chosen because it "directly measures whether the generated application behavior matches the reference implementation's intended functionality" (p. 4).
    63	- Maintainability M = (g/b)/(1+g/b), where g and b are the MI lower bounds of the generated and reference code. Called a "low-cost and reproducible signal of structural complexity"; the authors note that it misses naming quality and architectural clarity (p. 3).
    64	- Security S = min(1, (b+1)/(g+1)) over high-risk static findings, described as a "conservative risk signal" (p. 3).
    65	- Robustness Rb is the pass ratio of the robustness suite. Efficiency E = min(1, Tref/Tgen), set to 0 if the suite fails. Resource Ru is the mean of the capped memory and CPU ratios, set to 0 if the suite fails (p. 3; p. 4).
    66	- Non-functional score NF: AHP-weighted sum of the five dimensions (p. 4).
    67	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): [V] No significance tests, confidence intervals or effect sizes. The paper reports only means over 3 runs and Std/CV over 5 reruns (p. 5; p. 7). [V] Metric robustness is checked with Spearman rank correlation of model rankings under alternative aggregations (p. 10).
    68	
    69	## 7. Key findings
    70	1. [V] Functional correctness is low. The average functional score is 33.98% for standard and 30.23% for thinking LLMs, and no model exceeds 45%. Best: Gemini-3-Pro-Preview 43.86% and Gemini-2.5-Pro-Thinking 43.44%; lowest: DeepSeek-R1 16.23% (p. 5; p. 6).
    71	2. [V] Non-functional averages are higher: 52.25% for standard and 49.57% for thinking LLMs. For standard LLMs, average maintainability is 33.45% and security 87.40% (p. 5; p. 6).
    72	3. [V] NF separates models that functional scores do not: Gemini-2.5-Pro and GPT-4o have almost equal functional scores (27.63% vs 27.48%) but NF of 35.15% vs 57.59% (p. 5).
    73	4. [V] Thinking models are not consistently better and on average score slightly below standard LLMs (p. 6).
    74	5. [V] Failure taxonomy: requirement–implementation mismatches plus non-functional quality failures make up 82.8% of failures; executability/dependency failures make up 17.2% (p. 7).
    75	6. [V] Cost per run ranges from $0.15 (DeepSeek-V3.2) to $16.63 (Claude-3.7-Sonnet-Thinking), averaging $4.10 for standard and $11.00 for thinking models. Higher cost does not reliably buy a higher functional score (p. 8).
    76	7. [V] On GPT-5.2, none of the three one-shot strategies beat the baseline (41.80% functional, 57.10% NF). S1 scored 37.70/46.10, S2 40.20/49.90 and S3 41.20/49.60; all three lowered NF (p. 8; p. 9).
    77	8. [V] Prompt variants moved GPT-5.2's mean functional score from 0.4181 (baseline) to 0.4972 (clarified) and 0.4919 (paraphrased). The authors call the differences small (p. 9).
    78	9. [V] Functional scores had Std = 0 and CV = 0 across 5 reruns for all three models and all 38 projects; the median NF CV was 0.0007 (p. 6; p. 7).
    79	10. [V] The NF model ranking is stable under equal weights, uncapped normalisation and leave-one-out variants (Spearman 0.90–0.99), but not under a rank-based aggregate (0.6441) (p. 10).
    80	11. [V] Defect-injection sanity check: the functional suites detected all 76 injected defects (2 per task); the robustness suites detected 0.375 of them (p. 5).
    81	
    82	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
    83	- [A] The repositories are public, so pretraining exposure cannot be ruled out. Results are interpreted as reflecting "realistic public-repository exposure conditions" (p. 2).
    84	- [A] Validating tests on the reference repository supports oracle validity but does not guarantee full behavioural coverage (p. 3).
    85	- [A] MI does not capture naming quality or architectural clarity. Static security analysis can give false positives and false negatives. Runtime measures depend on the environment. The metrics are operational proxies, not an expert audit (p. 3; p. 4).
    86	- [A] The single-turn zero-shot protocol does not represent iterative or agentic workflows; a multi-turn/agentic study is future work (p. 4; p. 5).
    87	- [A] The strategy study (RQ4) uses a single model and is not a ranking of strategy families (p. 8).
    88	- [A] The AHP weights are not claimed to be universal across domains (p. 4).
    89	
    90	## 9. Limitations we identified
    91	- [I] The oracles are small. About 11 functional tests per task (p. 5) is a thin behavioural specification for projects of up to 109.5k LoC (p. 2). The 100% defect-detection rate rests on only 2 injected defects per task, and their type and injection method are not described (p. 5). It does not show that the suites would catch subtle divergences.
    92	- [I] Contamination is likely, not just possible. The example requirement in Fig. 2/3 asks for code that "is API-compatible with the core parts of the Stegano project" (p. 3; p. 4), naming the original even though project-specific names were supposedly removed (p. 2). In the Celery failure case, the generated code references `celery.utils.threads`, "consistent with upstream Celery internals" (p. 9), which suggests recall of the original code. Together with the supplied module/package surface (p. 4), the task partly tests memory of well-known Python libraries.
    93	- [I] The non-functional metrics can reward incomplete code. Maintainability and security are static and are computed whatever the functional result. A small or partial repository naturally has fewer high-risk findings and simpler structure. GPT-3.5-Turbo's 97.37% security score next to its 29.76% functional score (p. 6) fits this reading. NF therefore mixes "quality" with "less code". Only efficiency and resource are set to 0 when their suites fail (p. 3).
    94	- [I] The maintainability score M = (g/b)/(1+g/b) equals 0.5 when the generated MI equals the reference MI and approaches 1 only when the generated MI is much higher (p. 3). M is therefore on a different scale from the other four dimensions, yet it carries the largest weight (0.36) (p. 4). An average M of about 33% (p. 6) suggests that the typical generated repository has a lower MI lower bound than the reference, but the paper reports no raw MI values to confirm this.
    95	- [I] Zero variance in functional scores across 5 full reruns (p. 7) is surprising for API-served LLMs generating whole repositories, even with greedy decoding. Either the reruns re-evaluated cached generations, or the models were unusually deterministic. The paper does not say which, so the stability claim may describe the test harness rather than generation.
    96	- [I] The 446 repositories in the failure analysis (p. 7) do not match 16 models x 38 tasks (608 per run), and how they were selected is not reported. Who assigned the failure categories, and whether agreement was measured, is also not reported.
    97	- [I] The prompt-sensitivity result (0.4181 to 0.4972, about +8 points or +19% relative) (p. 9) is not "small" compared with the roughly 16-point spread across most models (p. 6). Requirement wording may matter as much as model choice.
    98	- [I] All projects are Python libraries or CLI-style tools (p. 2), with no GUI, web front end or interactive application, so the findings transfer only partly to UI-level reconstruction.
    99	- [I] "Maintainability" is reduced to one complexity index. Code smells, duplication, modularity and human judgement of the generated code are not measured.
   100	
   101	## 10. Threats to validity
   102	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] Requirements were drafted with access to the source code (p. 2), tests were built from the reference's documented behaviour (p. 2), and the interface specification reveals the module layout (p. 4). Contamination with the original public code is plausible (see section 9). Who drafted and reviewed the requirements and tests, and with what tool support, is not reported.
   103	- External (generalisability of sample/context): [I] 38 Python projects, mostly libraries and CLI tools. Generation is single-turn and zero-shot without agents (p. 4; p. 5), unlike vibe-coding practice where developers iterate with agents.
   104	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] The functional score is a pass rate on about 11 tests (p. 5), maintainability is the MI lower bound only (p. 3), and security is a count of high-risk static findings. These are weak proxies for "functional fidelity" and "maintainability" as our project defines them, which the authors acknowledge (p. 4).
   105	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] No tests or intervals. Model differences of a few points (e.g. 27.63 vs 27.48) are discussed only descriptively (p. 5). Results are means of three runs (p. 5).
   106	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [A] Code and data are public (p. 11), and commits are pinned (p. 2). [I] Decoding parameters appear only in the abstract, and the static-analysis tools are not named in the text.
   107	
   108	## 11. Future research directions
   109	- Stated by authors [A] (p. 10; p. 11):
   110	  - requirement analysis that turns short NL requests into explicit specifications with behaviours and edge cases;
   111	  - cross-module repair using application-level feedback;
   112	  - quality-aware generation that treats robustness, efficiency, resources, maintainability and security as explicit constraints;
   113	  - extending RAL-Bench to more projects and to multi-turn/agentic settings (p. 5).
   114	- Suggested by us [I]:
   115	  1. Run the same reference-validated test design in an agentic, iterative (vibe-coding-like) setting.
   116	  2. Report raw MI and add richer maintainability measures that do not depend on code size (smells, duplication, modularity, change-effort experiments).
   117	  3. Test with obfuscated project names and without the interface specification to estimate contamination.
   118	  4. Extend the design to applications with UIs.
   119	
   120	## 12. Relevance to our research
   121	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ2, RQ3, RQ4, RQ5 (secondary RQ1).
   122	- How it informs our work [I]: This is one of the few studies that measures both functional correctness and maintainability of the same generated applications against the original project, using the original as test oracle and as normalisation anchor. That is the joint fidelity-plus-quality design that RQ5 asks about. Its weaknesses (thin oracles, MI-only maintainability, single-turn generation, contamination) are exactly what a new study should improve. Its finding that one-shot repair and planning lowered non-functional quality (p. 8) is a direct warning for vibe-coding workflows that iterate on failures.
   123	
   124	## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
   125	| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
   126	|---|---|---|---|---|
   127	| RQ2 | In single-pass generation of 38 real Python applications, no LLM exceeds 45% functional test pass rate (averages 33.98% standard, 30.23% thinking). | p. 5 | V | weak (preprint, single study, ~11 tests/task) |
   128	| RQ2 | Most failures (82.8%) occur after the code runs (requirement–implementation mismatch or runtime instability); only 17.2% are executability/dependency failures. | p. 7 | V | weak (coding procedure not reported) |
   129	| RQ3 | Reference-normalised maintainability (MI lower bound) averages ~31–33%, the weakest non-functional dimension, while security averages 85–87%. | p. 6 | V | weak (single MI proxy; parity with reference scores only 0.5) |
   130	| RQ3 | On GPT-5.2, self-repair, environment repair and planning each lowered the aggregate non-functional score (46.1–49.9% vs 57.1% baseline) without raising functional correctness. | p. 8 | V | weak (one model, one-shot strategies) |
   131	| RQ4 | Tests are kept only if they pass on the pinned reference repository; functional suites caught 76/76 injected defects. | p. 2; p. 5 | V | weak (only 2 defects/task, method not described) |
   132	| RQ4 | Functional scores had zero variance across 5 reruns; the NF ranking is robust to weighting choices (Spearman ≥0.90) except rank-based aggregation (0.64). | p. 7; p. 10 | V | weak |
   133	| RQ4 | Authors cannot rule out pretraining exposure to the public reference repositories. | p. 2 | A | weak |
   134	| RQ4 | Giving the reference's module/package surface raised one task's functional score from 0.17 to 0.67, so interface hints strongly affect measured fidelity. | p. 4 | V | weak (single example) |
   135	| RQ5 | Authors propose quality-aware generation and multi-turn/agentic evaluation under the same benchmark as next steps. | p. 5; p. 10 | A | weak |
   136	
   137	## 14. Key quotes
   138	> "no model exceeds a 45% functional score" (p. 1)
   139	
   140	> "we do not claim that pretraining exposure can be fully ruled out" (p. 2)
   141	
   142	> "MI does not capture all aspects of maintainability, such as naming quality or architectural clarity" (p. 3)
   143	
   144	## Analyst notes
   145	- Reading coverage: whole paper read (pp. 1–12), including all tables and the reference list. Figure 4 (failure shares per category) is garbled in the text layer, so only the combined 82.8%/17.2% split stated in the text is used. Figure 6 (strategy workflows) was only skimmed.
   146	- Uncertainties:
   147	  - whether a "rerun" means regenerating the code or re-evaluating existing generations;
   148	  - how the 446 repositories were selected;
   149	  - which static-analysis tools were used;
   150	  - decoding settings (greedy decoding is stated only in the abstract).
   151	  
   152	  Model names such as GPT-5.2 and Gemini-3-Pro-Preview are taken as reported.
   153	- Strength ratings follow research-standards §5: a preprint without replication is rated weak, although the design (pinned references, reference-validated tests, repeated runs) would support "moderate" if published.

    17	
    18	# Design2Code: Benchmarking Multimodal Code Generation for Automated Front-End Engineering
    19	
    20	- Authors: Si, Chenglei; Zhang, Yanzhe; Li, Ryan; Yang, Zhengyuan; Liu, Ruibo; Yang, Diyi
    21	- Year / venue: 2025, Proceedings of the 2025 Conference of the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies (Volume 1: Long Papers) (published)
    22	- DOI: 10.18653/v1/2025.naacl-long.199 · URL: https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2025.naacl-long.199
    23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
    24	
    25	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
    26	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
    27	
    28	## 1. Research objective
    29	- Build the first real-world benchmark for converting a webpage screenshot (visual design) directly into HTML/CSS code with multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), with automatic visual-fidelity metrics and human evaluation, and use it to compare models and prompting methods [A] (p. 1).
    30	
    31	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
    32	- No formal RQs or hypotheses. Implicit questions: how well current MLLMs turn screenshots into code that renders into the reference page; whether text-augmented and self-revision prompting help; whether automatic metrics agree with human judgement; what makes a webpage hard [I] (based on sections 3–4, pp. 4–8).
    33	
    34	## 3. Methodology
    35	- Research design: benchmark construction plus comparative evaluation; automatic metric evaluation on all 484 test pages, human evaluation on a 100-page sample; regression analysis of metrics against human preferences [V] (pp. 2–7).
    36	- Approach / model / intervention: three prompting methods: (1) Direct prompting (screenshot + instruction to produce one HTML+CSS file); (2) Text-Augmented prompting (screenshot + all text extracted from the original page appended, to remove the OCR burden); (3) Self-Revision prompting (model sees reference screenshot, screenshot of its text-augmented output and that code, and is asked to revise) [V] (p. 4–5). Prompts explicitly say no JavaScript is needed for dynamic interactions [V] (p. 14). The authors also fine-tune their own Design2Code-18B (CogAgent-18B, LoRA rank 8, on a random 20% of WebSight v0.1) [V] (pp. 5, 15).
    37	- Baselines or comparison conditions: commercial GPT-4o, GPT-4V, Claude 3 Opus, Gemini 1.0 Pro Vision; open models LLaVA-V1.6-Mixtral-7B, DeepSeek-VL-7B, Idefics2-8B; fine-tuned WebSight VLM-8B and Design2Code-18B [V] (p. 5). On Design2Code-HARD: GPT-4o, GPT-4o Mini, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 3 Opus, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Gemini 1.5 Flash [V] (p. 8). Authors state comparisons are "not apple-to-apple" because of model size and training-data differences [A] (p. 5). Human pairwise comparisons use Gemini Pro Vision Direct as the single reference baseline [V] (p. 5).
    38	
    39	## 4. Dataset and sample
    40	- Data source(s): webpages linked from the C4 validation set; CSS embedded into one HTML file per page, giving 127.9k pages [V] (p. 2). Design2Code-HARD source is listed as "Real-World (GitHub)" in Table 4 (p. 14), while the main text says it uses "the same filtering process" (p. 8) — the exact origin of HARD pages is not further described [V] (pp. 8, 14).
    41	- Sample size (N) and unit: 484 webpages (test cases) [V] (p. 3); HARD: 80 webpages [V] (p. 8). Average 31,216 GPT-2 tokens per file (min 784, max 98,637), 158 tags on average, 84 HTML5 tag types, DOM depth 13 on average [V] (p. 3). Domain annotation on a random 25% subsample (N=120): company/org 27.7%, blog 25.3%, homepage 13.3% most common [V] (p. 3).
    42	- Sampling / selection method: automatic filtering (drop files >100k tokens, image-only or text-only layouts, deduplication) → 14k pages; strip external dependencies (script, iframe, svg, external links, href, media replaced by placeholders); first two authors manually curated a random 7k of the 14k for stand-alone rendering, no sensitive content and good formatting, after reaching 75% agreement on 200 jointly annotated pages → 484 pages; about one week of work [V] (pp. 2–3, 13). Diversity was sought "as possible" but no formal stratification is described [V] (p. 13).
    43	- Data availability (public? link?): authors state they release the dataset under the ODC-By license [A] (p. 10); no URL is given in our PDF [V] (p. 10).
    44	
    45	## 5. Experimental setup
    46	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: commercial models with greedy decoding and max 4,096 new tokens; model versions gpt-4o-2024-05-13, gpt-4-1106-vision-preview, claude-3-opus-20240229, gemini-1.0-pro-vision [V] (p. 14). Open models: temperature 0.5, repetition penalty 1.1; reference and generated screenshots concatenated into one image for single-image models; Qwen-VL-Chat and Mantis excluded because they failed to produce HTML in >80% of cases [V] (pp. 14–15). Fine-tuning: batch 32, lr 1e-5, 5,000 steps, 4× A6000 for about 2 days, checkpoint chosen on a 20-example dev set [V] (p. 15). Gemini 1.5 gave empty responses in the main experiment [V] (p. 14). Human evaluators: Prolific, US only, ≥2,500 surveys with ≥98% pass rate, 60 participants, $16/hour, 5 annotators per item, majority vote [V] (pp. 5, 15).
    47	- Code availability: authors promise "clear ethical use guidelines for all data, code, and model releases" [A] (p. 10); no repository link in our PDF — not reported.
    48	
    49	## 6. Evaluation metrics
    50	- High-level visual similarity — CLIP(IR, IG): cosine similarity of CLIP-ViT-B/32 embeddings of the reference and rendered screenshots after resizing to squares, with text regions in-painted (Telea) to remove text [V] (p. 3).
    51	- Low-level element matching, after detecting text blocks in both screenshots (by recolouring text segments in the HTML and tracking pixels, not OCR) and matching them with the Jonker-Volgenant algorithm on text similarity (pairs with similarity <0.5 ignored; neighbouring blocks may be merged) [V] (pp. 4, 13):
    52	  - Block-Match — share of total block area covered by matched blocks; unmatched (missing or hallucinated) blocks lower it — measures element recall/precision [V] (pp. 4–5).
    53	  - Text — character-level Sørensen-Dice similarity of matched blocks, averaged [V] (p. 4).
    54	  - Position — 1 − max(|Δx|, |Δy|) of normalised block centres, averaged [V] (p. 4).
    55	  - Color — CIEDE2000 perceptual colour difference of text in matched blocks, averaged [V] (p. 4).
    56	  - Why chosen: text-based code similarity (edit distance, htmlBLEU) cannot judge visual result because many different codes render the same page [A] (p. 3).
    57	- Human evaluation: (a) pairwise Win/Tie/Lose vs Gemini Pro Vision Direct on 100 sampled pages, priority content > layout > style; (b) direct assessment of GPT-4V self-revision outputs: "can it replace the original?" and "which is better designed?" [V] (pp. 5–6, 15–16).
    58	- Validation against human judgement: logistic regression on metric differences predicting Win/Lose, 50/50 split of the 100 annotated pages, 435 pairwise annotations, 79.9% test accuracy; coefficients Block-Match 0.7429, Position 0.7605, CLIP 0.4929, Color 0.3461 (all p ≤ 0.001), Text −0.3541 (p = 0.021) [V] (p. 7). Simulated win rates from a refit linear model (text removed) correlate with human "win + tie" rates across 10 systems: Pearson r = 0.975, Kendall τ = 0.931 [V] (p. 17). Inter-annotator agreement: Fleiss' κ = 0.46 (pairwise), 0.32 (replaceability), 0.26 (which is better) [V] (p. 16).
    59	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): only regression coefficient p-values and correlation significance (Table 7, p < 0.05 marks) [V] (pp. 7, 15). No significance tests, confidence intervals or variance across runs for model comparisons — not reported.
    60	
    61	## 7. Key findings
    62	1. GPT-4o is best on every automatic dimension (Direct: Block 93.0, Text 98.2, Position 85.5, Color 84.1, CLIP 90.4) [V] (p. 6); in human pairwise evaluation GPT-4o Direct wins 92% vs the Gemini baseline [V] (p. 7).
    63	2. Text-augmented prompting raises Block-Match and Text for most models (e.g. GPT-4V Block 85.8 → 87.6; Gemini 80.2 → 84.8); self-revision helps GPT-4V and Claude 3 a little and does not help Gemini or open models (DeepSeek-VL self-revision collapses to Block 30.1) [V] (pp. 5–6).
    64	3. Main weakness: models "mostly lag in recalling visual elements ... and generating correct layout designs" [A] (p. 1); on Design2Code-HARD, state-of-the-art models miss 30–40% of block elements (GPT-4o Direct Block 56.6) [V] (p. 8).
    65	4. Fine-tuned open models (WebSight VLM-8B, Design2Code-18B) roughly match Gemini 1.0 Pro Vision Direct (Block 55.9 / 78.5 vs 80.2; CLIP 87.6 / 85.8 vs 84.4) [V] (p. 6).
    66	5. Direct assessment: 49% of GPT-4V self-revision pages judged interchangeable with the reference; generated pages preferred over the original in 64% of cases [V] (p. 6). Kappa for these questions is low (0.32, 0.26) [V] (p. 16).
    67	6. Humans weight high-level layout and presence of content, not exact text: text similarity has a negative coefficient in predicting preference [V] (p. 7). Human and automatic rankings disagree in places (e.g. humans prefer WebSight VLM-8B over Design2Code-18B despite worse Block-Match/Text) [V] (pp. 6–7).
    68	7. Total tag count is the strongest difficulty indicator (r = −0.28 with Block-Match for GPT-4V self-revision); non-English pages are harder [V] (pp. 8, 15).
    69	8. Code quality, maintainability or functional behaviour of the generated code is not measured; all metrics are visual/textual on rendered screenshots [V] (pp. 3–4).
    70	
    71	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
    72	- Better prompting is needed for complex pages, e.g. incremental generation of page parts [A] (p. 10).
    73	- Training directly on real webpages is hard because they are long and noisy [A] (p. 10).
    74	- Input is screenshot-only; Figma frames or sketches would need a re-designed evaluation [A] (p. 10).
    75	- Only static webpages; dynamic pages need evaluation of "interactive functions beyond just visual similarity" [A] (p. 10).
    76	- Human evaluation should not be "blindly trusted as the oracle" because of human top-down attention bias [A] (pp. 7–8).
    77	- Text-block matching may be imperfect when granularity differs (non-contiguous merges not searched) [A] (p. 13).
    78	
    79	## 9. Limitations we identified
    80	- [I] Fidelity is purely visual (screenshot similarity). No functional, behavioural, or code-level quality measure (e.g. HTML validity, semantic structure, maintainability, responsiveness) — based on metric definitions pp. 3–4. For our project this means Design2Code says nothing about whether a rebuilt page works or is maintainable.
    81	- [I] JavaScript, iframes, SVG and external links are stripped and prompts say no JS is needed (pp. 13–14); the task is reconstruction of a static, de-functionalised snapshot, not of an application.
    82	- [I] Human validation is modest: 100 pages, Fleiss' κ only 0.46/0.32/0.26 (p. 16), logistic regression accuracy 79.9% on a 50-page test half (p. 7). The very high Pearson r = 0.975 is computed over only 10 system-level points (p. 17) and compares predicted wins with human "win + tie" — an aggregation that inflates agreement.
    83	- [I] Test pages come from C4, a common pretraining corpus; data contamination is not discussed (grep for "contamin" finds nothing).
    84	- [I] Single run per configuration with greedy decoding; no variance or significance testing between models (pp. 5–6, 14).
    85	- [I] Design2Code-HARD origin is inconsistent: "same filtering process" (p. 8) vs source "GitHub" (p. 14).
    86	- [I] Element metrics are text-anchored (blocks come from text segments, p. 13); images, icons and non-text elements are only covered by CLIP.
    87	
    88	## 10. Threats to validity
    89	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): manual curation by the authors (selection bias towards well-formatted pages) (p. 13); possible C4 pretraining contamination (not discussed); Design2Code-18B checkpoint chosen on a 20-example dev set (p. 15) [I].
    90	- External (generalisability of sample/context): static, single-page, English-dominant web pages with placeholders for media; HARD set of 80 (p. 8); no mobile apps, multi-page or interactive apps [I].
    91	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): metrics measure visual similarity of a rendered screenshot, not functional fidelity or code quality; Text metric is negatively associated with human preference (p. 7), so the five metrics do not all point the same way [I].
    92	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): no CIs or tests for model differences; low-moderate inter-annotator agreement (p. 16); system-level correlation on n = 10 (p. 17) [I].
    93	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): prompts, model versions and decoding settings reported (p. 14); fine-tuning hyper-parameters reported (p. 15); dataset release claimed but no link in our PDF (p. 10); commercial model versions may be deprecated [I].
    94	
    95	## 11. Future research directions
    96	- Stated by authors [A]: incremental generation for complex pages; cleaning pipelines for training on real webpages; Figma/sketch inputs; dynamic webpages with interactive-function evaluation (p. 10); "generate UIs that support dynamic user interactions" (p. 9); website-design improvement tools (p. 6).
    97	- Suggested by us [I]: pair the visual metrics with behavioural tests and static code-quality analysis of the generated HTML/CSS; report run-to-run variance; check pretraining contamination of C4-sourced pages.
    98	
    99	## 12. Relevance to our research
   100	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ2, RQ4, RQ5 (RQ3 only by absence).
   101	- How it informs our work [I]: Design2Code is the reference benchmark for screenshot-to-code reconstruction and the origin of the Block/Text/Position/Color/CLIP metric family reused by later work. It shows how visual fidelity can be measured and partly validated against humans, and it clearly leaves out interaction, functionality and code quality — the dimensions our project needs.
   102	
   103	## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
   104	| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
   105	|---|---|---|---|---|
   106	| RQ1 | Screenshot-to-HTML/CSS with MLLMs via direct, text-augmented and self-revision prompting, plus fine-tuned open models | p. 4–5 | V | moderate |
   107	| RQ2 | Visual fidelity measured by Block-Match, Text, Position, Color (CIEDE2000) and CLIP on rendered screenshots | p. 3–5 | V | moderate |
   108	| RQ2 | GPT-4o Direct best: Block 93.0, Text 98.2, Position 85.5, Color 84.1, CLIP 90.4 on 484 pages | p. 6 | V | moderate |
   109	| RQ2 | On 80 HARD pages SOTA models miss 30–40% of blocks (GPT-4o Direct Block 56.6) | p. 8 | V | moderate |
   110	| RQ2 | 49% of GPT-4V self-revision pages judged interchangeable with the original (κ = 0.32) | p. 6, 16 | V | weak |
   111	| RQ3 | No code quality or maintainability measure; only rendered visual similarity | p. 3–4 | V | moderate |
   112	| RQ4 | Metrics predict human Win/Lose with 79.9% accuracy (logistic regression, 50-page test half); Text coefficient negative | p. 7 | V | moderate |
   113	| RQ4 | Simulated vs human win rates: Pearson r = 0.975, Kendall τ = 0.931 over 10 systems | p. 17 | V | weak |
   114	| RQ4 | Human agreement low-moderate: Fleiss' κ 0.46 / 0.32 / 0.26 | p. 16 | V | moderate |
   115	| RQ4 | No significance tests or variance across runs for model comparisons | p. 5–6 | I | moderate |
   116	| RQ5 | Authors call for dynamic webpages evaluated on interactive functions beyond visual similarity | p. 10 | A | moderate |
   117	
   118	## 14. Key quotes
   119	> "models mostly lag in recalling visual elements from the input webpages and generating correct layout designs" (p. 1)
   120	> "We find that 49% of the AI-generated webpages are considered exchangeable with the reference webpages." (p. 6)
   121	> "This also requires the evaluation to consider interactive functions beyond just visual similarity." (p. 10)
   122	
   123	## Analyst notes
   124	- Reading coverage: whole PDF read (pp. 1–19), including appendices A–I; reference list skimmed only.
   125	- Uncertainties: dataset/code URL not given in our ACL PDF (the arXiv version may differ); HARD-set source inconsistent between p. 8 and p. 14; the logistic-regression test-set size in pairs is not stated separately (435 is the total of usable pairs). Peer-reviewed (NAACL 2025, tier 1).

    17	
    18	# Vibe Code Bench: Evaluating AI Models on End-to-End Web Application Development
    19	
    20	- Authors: Tran, Hung; Nashold, Langston; Krishnan, Rayan; Bigeard, Antoine; Gu, Alex
    21	- Year / venue: 2026, Proceedings of the ACM Conference on AI and Agentic Systems (published)
    22	- DOI: 10.1145/3786335.3813180 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1145/3786335.3813180
    23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
    24	
    25	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
    26	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
    27	
    28	## 1. Research objective
    29	[A] To measure whether LLMs can carry out the complete "zero-to-one" process of building a working, deployable web application from a natural-language specification alone, judged by user-visible behaviour, and to check how reliable automated browser-agent evaluation is (p. 1, p. 3).
    30	
    31	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
    32	No formal RQs or hypotheses. Stated contributions (p. 1–2):
    33	- [A] A benchmark and browser-based evaluation pipeline for end-to-end web-app development (p. 1).
    34	- [A] A comparison of 16 frontier models including cost, latency and error analysis (p. 1–2).
    35	- [A] An evaluator-alignment protocol with cross-model and human annotation (p. 2).
    36	
    37	## 3. Methodology
    38	- Research design: benchmark construction plus a comparative evaluation of 16 models in one fixed agent harness; secondary analyses (tool use, error taxonomy, reasoning-effort and vision ablations, variance decomposition, human-alignment study) (p. 4–9). [V]
    39	- Approach / model / intervention: each model receives only a non-technical text specification and builds the app from scratch inside a modified OpenHands container with terminal, browser, Supabase/MailHog/Stripe services and MCP tools, up to 5 hours wall-clock per app (p. 3–4). [V] The system prompt mandates React + Vite, Tailwind, Supabase and Docker Compose (p. 4, p. 16). [V] The authors say a fixed stack was needed because otherwise apps "were too heterogeneous to evaluate consistently at scale" (p. 4). [A]
    40	- How functional correctness is tested: pre-authored natural-language UI workflows (6–23 per task, each with substeps) are executed by an autonomous Browser Use agent (canonical evaluator model Claude Sonnet 4.5, vision on, headless 1920×1200, max 100 steps per workflow) against the deployed app; the agent produces pass/fail per substep ("LLM-as-judge substep judgments"); a workflow passes when ≥ 90% of substeps succeed; app accuracy = share of passing workflows (p. 4–5, p. 15). [V] If deployment fails, all workflows fail (p. 5). [V] The evaluator follows fixed workflow definitions rather than generating tests on the fly (p. 4). [V] Fresh browser session and unique account data per workflow to stop state leaking between tests (p. 5). [V]
    41	- Baselines or comparison conditions: 16 models from 9 providers compared with each other; no human-developer or commercial-tool baseline (p. 5). [V]
    42	
    43	## 4. Dataset and sample
    44	- Data source(s): task ideas inspired by consumer apps, YC startup ideas, consulting case studies and internal enterprise needs; specifications and 6–23 draft workflows generated by a structured-output GPT-5 pipeline; two-pass review by two PM reviewers (Accept/Modify/Reject per test); PM line review plus an LLM-based audit for spec/test misalignment before freeze (p. 3). [V]
    45	- Sample size (N) and unit: 100 specifications (24 Individual, 45 Solo Founder, 31 Enterprise Tool), 964 workflows, 10,131 substeps; test split 50 apps / 473 workflows / 5,136 substeps (p. 3–4, Table 3). [V] 28/100 apps need Stripe and/or email (p. 3). [V] Test-split difficulty tiers: Easy 23, Medium 19, Hard 8 (p. 6, Table 5). [V]
    46	- Sampling / selection method: expert-designed, not sampled from a population of real apps; selection criteria beyond the idea sources are not reported (p. 3). [V] Difficulty tiers are assigned after the fact from mean pass rate across the 16 models (p. 6). [V]
    47	- Data availability (public? link?): harness fork and all trajectories/generated apps released on GitHub (p. 11). [A] Whether the test-split specifications and workflows are public is not stated; the text calls validation "private" (p. 1, p. 3) while Table 3 labels it "Validation (public)" (p. 4). [V]
    48	
    49	## 5. Experimental setup
    50	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: per-model temperature, top-p, reasoning level and vision flag listed (p. 15, Table 15); highest reasoning level and provider default temperature (p. 5); GLM-5, MiniMax M2.5 and DeepSeek V3.2 ran without usable browser vision (p. 5, p. 15). [V] Same retry policy for all runs (p. 15). [V] Evaluator hyper-parameters (timeouts, step caps, 90% threshold) in Table 16 (p. 15). [V] Main results use one generation per model per app (the variance study is the only multi-run experiment, p. 8). [V]
    51	- Code availability: harness and artifacts on GitHub (p. 11). [A] Full generation system prompt, an example spec and an example UI-test file are printed (p. 16–23). [V]
    52	- Evaluator-reliability design: (a) variance panel — 6 specs x 3 source models x 5 independent generations (90 generations), and the same frozen apps re-evaluated 5 times (90 evaluations) (p. 8); (b) human alignment — 6 tasks x 3 source models = 18 apps, 1,401 substeps; each app evaluated by two of three human evaluators who used only the browser, were calibrated on a practice question and were blind to model and to other evaluators' scores; four evaluator models each ran once per app; no adjudication (p. 8–9). [V]
    53	
    54	## 6. Evaluation metrics
    55	- Accuracy — percentage of workflows passing (≥ 90% substeps) — chosen to tolerate minor non-critical errors and avoid credit from unrelated workflows ("cross-workflow masking") (p. 5). [V]/[A]
    56	- Cost (API cost of generation, caching included) and latency (wall-clock generation time) (p. 5). [V]
    57	- Pairwise step-level agreement — share of substeps where two evaluators give the same pass/fail (p. 9). [V] No chance-corrected statistic (e.g. Cohen's kappa) is reported. [V] (p. 9)
    58	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): mean ± standard error across the 50 test apps (p. 5); Pearson correlations between tool use and accuracy across 16 models (p. 7); variance decomposition into generation vs evaluator share (p. 8). No significance tests for model differences. [V]
    59	
    60	## 7. Key findings
    61	1. Top test-split accuracy: GPT-5.3-Codex 61.77 ± 4.71%, Claude Opus 4.6 57.57 ± 4.37%, GPT-5.2 53.50 ± 5.07%; lowest Grok 4.1 Fast Reasoning 1.20 ± 1.20% (p. 6, Table 4). [V] Open-weight models range ~5–23% (p. 6, Table 4). [V]
    62	2. Accuracy falls with difficulty (all-model average 44.29% easy, 21.36% medium, 6.03% hard) and with external integrations (34.18% none vs 13.49% email + Stripe) (p. 6, Tables 5–6). [V] Average by domain: Individual 43.01%, Solo Founder 29.94%, Enterprise Tool 18.64% (p. 7, Table 7). [V]
    63	3. Browser tool calls per app correlate with accuracy across the 16 models (Pearson r = 0.72; partial r = 0.72 controlling for latency); edit calls barely correlate (r = 0.09) (p. 7). [V] The authors interpret this as self-testing being associated with better outcomes (p. 7). [A]
    64	4. Failures are mostly zero-score apps: 12.8% of apps score zero for the top five models vs 73.2% for the bottom five; 14.0% of apps from the worst five fail to start; only 8.8% of top-five apps score 100% (p. 7). [V]
    65	5. Behavioural failure taxonomy (apps that started): missing feature 46.7%, authorization 20.4%, validation/policy block 14.8%, UI rendering/navigation 6.0%, data consistency/backend 1.9%, other 10.2% (p. 8). [V] How failures were classified (human or LLM) is not reported.
    66	6. Variance: generation-side variance dominates (92.5%, 92.1%, 73.5% of observed variance for Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4.6); evaluator rerun SE 0.99–3.00 pp vs generation SE 3.47–5.00 pp (p. 8, Table 9). [V] The authors conclude rankings are robust except for near-ties (p. 8). [A]
    67	7. Human–human step agreement 88.6–93.6%; Claude Sonnet 4.5 (canonical evaluator) 86.4% mean agreement with humans, Claude Sonnet 4.6 86.3%, Gemini 3.1 Pro 84.7%, GPT-5.2 only 36.1% (p. 9, Table 10). [V] Model–model agreement ranges 33.1–87.8% (p. 9). [V]
    68	8. Vibe Code Bench separates models more than SWE-Bench: MiniMax M2.5 vs Claude Opus 4.6 gap 2.8% on SWE-Bench vs 42.7% on VCB (p. 2). [V] (57.57 − 14.85 = 42.72, consistent with Table 4.)
    69	
    70	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
    71	- [A] Design and code quality not measured: no evaluation of code readability, visual design quality or security vulnerabilities; passing functional tests does not imply maintainable, secure or documented code (p. 9).
    72	- [A] Single OpenHands-based harness; other harnesses might score higher (p. 9).
    73	- [A] Single technology stack (React/Vite + Supabase); results may not generalise to other stacks (p. 9).
    74	- [A] Web applications only; CLI, desktop and mobile apps unexplored (p. 9).
    75	- [A] Three models ran without browser vision because of provider configuration (p. 5).
    76	
    77	## 9. Limitations we identified
    78	- [I] Functional fidelity is judged by an LLM browser agent, and the canonical evaluator (Claude Sonnet 4.5) belongs to the same family as several evaluated models (Claude Opus/Sonnet/Haiku). Self-preference or style-familiarity bias is not tested: alignment was measured only on apps from Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT-5.2 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 (p. 8–9), and per-source-model agreement is not reported.
    79	- [I] Agreement is raw percent agreement with no chance correction (p. 9). If most substeps pass or most fail, high percent agreement can coexist with low kappa. The very low GPT-5.2 agreement (31.8–48.0% with every other evaluator) is unexplained; agreement this far below the 84–94% of the other pairs implies GPT-5.2 labels largely the opposite way (e.g. mostly "fail" where others say "pass"), which points to a systematic problem (such as runs without structured output counted as fails) rather than ordinary judgment disagreement. Based on Table 10 (p. 9) and failure semantics (p. 5).
    80	- [I] The alignment panel is small (18 apps from 6 tasks) relative to 50 test apps x 16 models; agreement is reported at substep level, while the leaderboard uses workflow-level pass with a 90% threshold. Workflow-level human–model agreement is not reported (p. 5, p. 9).
    81	- [I] Main leaderboard numbers come from a single generation per model per app; ± SE reflects variation across apps, not across runs (p. 5, p. 8). Generation variance is large (SE up to 5 pp on the 6-app panel, p. 8), so adjacent ranks (e.g. GPT-5.2 vs Opus 4.6 Thinking, both 53.50) are not separable.
    82	- [I] Specifications and workflows were drafted by GPT-5 (p. 3); a possible advantage for OpenAI models (top rank) is not examined.
    83	- [I] The self-testing correlation is across only 16 models and is observational; the system prompt itself demands browser testing (p. 16, p. 19), so browser-call counts may reflect instruction following as much as testing skill. Identical r and partial r (both 0.72, p. 7) are reported without explanation.
    84	- [I] Difficulty tiers are defined from the evaluated models' own pass rates (p. 6), so tier results are partly circular.
    85	- [I] The error taxonomy procedure (who labelled, how many failures) is not described (p. 8).
    86	- [I] Authors are mostly from Vals AI, a company (p. 1); funding and conflicts are not reported. Not a model vendor, so no direct ranking conflict is visible.
    87	- [I] The validation split is called "private" in the text (p. 1, p. 3) but "public" in Table 3 (p. 4); public availability of test tasks (and thus future contamination risk) is unclear.
    88	
    89	## 10. Threats to validity
    90	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): mandated tech stack and prompt reduce heterogeneity but make results harness- and prompt-specific (p. 4, p. 9) [V]. Evaluator same-family bias not tested [I]. Test-isolation measures reported (p. 5) [V].
    91	- External (generalisability of sample/context): 100 expert-written greenfield specs, one stack, web only (p. 3, p. 9) [V]. Tasks start from a text spec, not from an existing app's UI or behaviour, so results transfer to reconstruction only indirectly [I].
    92	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): browser workflows measure user-visible functional behaviour and are implementation-agnostic (p. 3–4) [V]; they do not capture code quality, security, visual fidelity or maintainability (p. 9) [V]. The 90% substep threshold is a design choice without sensitivity analysis [I] (p. 5).
    93	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): SE across 50 apps reported; variance decomposition on 6 apps x 3 models (p. 5, p. 8) [V]; no significance tests; correlations with n = 16 [I].
    94	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): unusually complete — prompts, hyper-parameters, evaluator settings, harness and trajectories released (p. 11, p. 15–23) [V]; evaluator uses LLM sampling without fixed seed ("none set in evaluator code", p. 15) [V].
    95	
    96	## 11. Future research directions
    97	- Stated by authors [A]: extending "zero-to-one" evaluation to CLI, desktop and mobile apps; testing other harnesses and stacks; measuring readability, visual design and security (implied by the limitations list, p. 9). Treat evaluator choice as "a first-class reporting concern" (p. 9).
    98	- Suggested by us [I]: reuse the browser-workflow oracle for reconstruction tasks — run the same workflows on the original app and the rebuilt app to score behavioural fidelity; add static-analysis and maintainability metrics on the generated repositories (which the authors release); report chance-corrected agreement and workflow-level human–judge agreement.
    99	
   100	## 12. Relevance to our research
   101	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (agentic vibe-coding generation of full web apps from text specs), RQ2 (functional fidelity via browser workflows; headline accuracy), RQ3 (explicitly not measured — useful as negative evidence), RQ4 (LLM-judge reliability, human alignment, variance decomposition), RQ5 (authors' own call for code-quality measurement).
   102	- How it informs our work [I]: This is the closest benchmark to a vibe-coding rebuild: a non-technical spec in, a deployed multi-page app out, judged only through the browser like a user. Its evaluation design (pre-authored natural-language workflows run by a browser agent, with a human-alignment check) is a ready template for measuring functional fidelity of a reconstructed app against the original. It also shows that the judge itself is a major source of measurement error (36% vs 86% human agreement depending on judge model), and that code quality and maintainability remain unmeasured.
   103	
   104	## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
   105	| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
   106	|---|---|---|---|---|
   107	| RQ2 | Best of 16 models (GPT-5.3-Codex) passes 61.77 ± 4.71% of browser workflows for web apps built from scratch from a text spec (50 test apps) | 6 | V | moderate |
   108	| RQ2 | Functional success drops with difficulty (avg 44.3% easy vs 6.0% hard) and with external services (34.2% none vs 13.5% email + Stripe) | 6 | V | moderate |
   109	| RQ2 | Most failed workflows (apps that started) are missing features (46.7%) or authorization problems (20.4%) | 8 | V | weak |
   110	| RQ1 | Browser self-testing during generation correlates with accuracy across 16 models (r = 0.72), edit volume does not (r = 0.09) | 7 | V | weak |
   111	| RQ4 | Functional fidelity is scored by an LLM browser agent (Claude Sonnet 4.5) running pre-authored NL workflows; workflow passes at ≥90% substeps | 4 | V | moderate |
   112	| RQ4 | Human–human substep agreement is 88.6–93.6%; judge–human agreement ranges 36.1% (GPT-5.2) to 86.4% (Claude Sonnet 4.5) on 18 apps / 1,401 substeps; raw agreement only, no kappa | 9 | V | moderate |
   113	| RQ4 | Generation variance dominates evaluator variance (73.5–92.5% of variance) on a 6-app x 3-model x 5-run panel | 8 | V | weak |
   114	| RQ3 | Code readability, security and visual design quality of the generated apps are not measured | 9 | A | strong |
   115	| RQ5 | Authors state passing functional tests does not imply maintainable, secure or documented code | 9 | A | moderate |
   116	
   117	## 14. Key quotes
   118	> "Passing functional tests does not imply maintainable, secure, or well-documented code." (p. 9)
   119	> "This indicates evaluator outputs are not interchangeable, and evaluator selection can materially change reported outcomes." (p. 9)
   120	> "We use Claude Sonnet 4.5 as the canonical evaluator for this benchmark" (p. 4)
   121	
   122	## Analyst notes
   123	- Reading coverage: whole paper read: main text p. 1–9, references p. 10, appendices A–I p. 11–23 (artifacts, histograms, all-model tables, tools, hyper-parameters, system prompt, spec and UI-test examples). Figures 3–8 (plots) are not readable from the text layer; only values stated in the text are used. Reasoning-effort and vision ablation numbers (Figures 4–5) are not reported in text.
   124	- Uncertainties: meaning of "Evaluator Acc." in Table 9 (e.g. Gemini 3.1 Pro 37.61% vs generation 19.38%) is not explained (p. 8); it probably refers to re-scoring one frozen generation, but the paper does not say which. Partial r equal to r (0.72) is reported without explanation. Validation split "private" vs "public" inconsistency (p. 1/3 vs p. 4). Proceedings of the ACM Conference on AI and Agentic Systems published
Code generation has emerged as one of AI’s highest-impact use cases, yet existing benchmarks measure isolated tasks rather than the complete "zero-to-one" process of building a working application from scratch. We introduce Vibe Code Bench, a benchmark of 100 web application specifications (50 public validation, 50 held-out test) with 964 browser-based workflows comprising 10,131 substeps, evaluated against deployed applications by an autonomous browser agent.

1	---
     2	key: wu2026looks
     3	status: ready
     4	evidence_basis: full-text
     5	design: benchmark construction + five-axis empirical evaluation of six frontier MLLMs in a fixed single-agent harness; VLM-judge validation; failure taxonomy on labelled sample
     6	dataset: MobileForge: 29 in-market consumer mobile apps, 309 human-reviewed screenshots, page-relationship annotations, 701 navigation test specifications
     7	sample_size: 29 apps x 6 models = 174 runs (single trial each); 701 navigation specs; 55 human-ranked scenarios; 64 hand-labelled failures
     8	metrics: Build success (tsc+vite), NavPassRate (state-isolated Playwright tests), list-wise Borda visual score (anchor-referenced VLM judge) + point-wise rubric, LoC, LoC/file, ReuseRate, DeadCompRate, ColorConsistency, tokens/cost
     9	main_finding: All models build multi-screen React apps; navigation 58-92% pass; visual fidelity <=2.99/5; visual leader (Opus 4.6) is not maintainability leader (GPT-5).
    10	relevance: high
    11	analysed: 2026-11-11
    12	---
    13	<!-- Frontmatter: single-line values; they feed literature-matrix.md via `rlab index`.
    14	     status: draft (in progress) -> ready (analyst self-check passed) -> complete (critical review passed).
    15	     evidence_basis: full-text | abstract-only. abstract-only analyses must not fill methodology detail.
    16	     relevance: high | medium | low. -->
    17	
    18	# Looks Right, Works Right: A Project-Level Benchmark for Multi-Screen Mobile App Generation
    19	
    20	- Authors: Wu, Fan; Gao, Cuiyun; Huang, Yiming; Xiao, Yang; Chen, Yujia; Liao, Qing
    21	- Year / venue: 2026, Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (published)
    22	- DOI: 10.18653/2026.emnlp-main.2650 · URL: https://doi.org/10.18653/2026.emnlp-main.2650
    23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
    24	
    25	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
    26	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
    27	
    28	## 1. Research objective
    29	- Introduce MobileForge, a benchmark for project-level multi-screen mobile app generation from a folder of real app screenshots, with a five-axis evaluation (build, navigation, visual fidelity, code maintainability, efficiency), and use it to measure how far frontier multimodal LLMs are from producing a buildable, navigable, faithful and maintainable codebase [A] (pp. 1–2).
    30	
    31	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
    32	- Opening question: "Can a multimodal LLM read a folder of mobile-app screenshots and generate the source code for that app?" [V] (p. 1). No formal hypotheses. The paper targets three gaps of existing benchmarks: single-page focus, no evaluation of interactive navigation, no project-wide maintainability measure [A] (p. 1).
    33	
    34	## 3. Methodology
    35	- Research design: benchmark construction (VLM-drafted, human-reviewed annotations) plus a full-factorial evaluation of 6 models × 29 apps with a fixed agentic harness, single trial per cell; method studies of the visual judge (human alignment, cross-judge, protocol comparison); hand-labelled failure taxonomy [V] (pp. 3–8, 12–13).
    36	- Approach / model / intervention: one tool-augmented agent receives all screenshots of an app plus the human-reviewed page-relationship description and must produce a React + TypeScript + Tailwind project in a pre-scaffolded directory; eight tools (write_file, read_file, str_replace, batch_str_replace, list_files, delete_file, run_command, task_done), soft six-phase plan, up to 50 iterations; on task_done an automated tsc + vite build feeds errors back [V] (p. 6). Prompting is fixed across models, with no screenshot-specific instructions or chain-of-thought, to attribute differences to the model [A] (pp. 6, 14).
    37	- Baselines or comparison conditions: six closed models available April 2026 — Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Haiku 4.5, GPT-5, GPT-5 Mini, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Gemini 2.5 Flash [V] (p. 6). No open-weight models and no non-agentic or prior-method baselines [I] (based on p. 6).
    38	
    39	## 4. Dataset and sample
    40	- Data source(s): 29 in-market consumer apps from official public distribution channels; screenshots captured manually from default-state or demo-mode screens without logging in [V] (pp. 3, 9).
    41	- Sample size (N) and unit: 29 apps across 14 category buckets; 309 screens (mean 10.7, SD 3.8, range 5–21 per app); 701 navigation test specifications (mean 24.2, range 11–41 per app): 120 page-existence, 392 tab-navigation, 189 parent–child [V] (p. 3). Apps include Notion, Khan Academy, WhatsApp, Klook, Airbnb, Coinbase and others (Table 5) [V] (p. 12).
    42	- Sampling / selection method: apps "prioritizing broad cultural recognition" [V] (p. 3) — a purposive, not random, selection. Annotation: a VLM drafts the page-relationship description and test specs; research-team annotators review every field; auto-drafts reach 96.8% recall / 94.3% precision (pages) and 74.1% / 83.9% (test cases); 64.7% of page and 76.5% of test drafts accepted unchanged [V] (pp. 3, 9, 15). The drafting VLM is not named — not reported. Inter-annotator agreement — not reported.
    43	- Data availability (public? link?): https://github.com/anoa12159-hue/mobileforge_eval, research-only licence, with screenshots, annotations, harness, evaluator and all 174 run artifacts [A] (pp. 1, 9–10).
    44	
    45	## 5. Experimental setup
    46	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: single trial per (app, model) cell, 174 runs all completed [V] (p. 6). Build: clean Vite scaffold (React 19 + TypeScript + Tailwind), `npx tsc --noEmit` and `vite build` must both pass with zero errors [V] (p. 4). Navigation tests run in headless Playwright (375×812 viewport) [V] (p. 5). Visual judge: Gemini 2.5 Pro, list-wise with k-shuffle = 3 and reference anchor over 29 apps × 701 scenarios [V] (pp. 6, 13). Sampling temperature and other decoding settings — not reported.
    47	- Code availability: repository above; "one-command replay reproduces the comparison table verbatim" [A] (p. 10). Full system prompt only in the repository [V] (p. 14).
    48	
    49	## 6. Evaluation metrics
    50	- Build Success — both type-check and build pass; also route count, page-file count, route coverage [V] (p. 4).
    51	- Navigation Correctness — NavPassRate: share of the 701 specs passed under state-isolated execution: each test starts by loading the source page route directly, performs the action, and passes if the URL matches the expected page or, for overlays, the page content hash "changes meaningfully" [V] (pp. 4–5). Rationale: chained walkthroughs cascade failures and blur attribution [A] (p. 5).
    52	- Visual Fidelity — primary: per-model Borda score in [0, 1] from list-wise ranking by a VLM judge, with the original screenshot hidden among candidates as an anchor; rankings where the anchor is not first are discarded and re-run [V] (pp. 4–6). Secondary: point-wise 1–5 rubric (Layout 30%, Style 25%, Content 25%, Consistency 20%) kept as an absolute reference [V] (p. 6).
    53	- Code Maintainability — total LoC; mean LoC/file (conciseness); ReuseRate (mean import count per shared component); DeadCompRate (share of declared components never imported); ColorConsistency (share of Tailwind colour tokens from a small recurring palette) [V] (p. 4). The authors use "maintainability" rather than "code quality" because correctness is covered by Build [A] (p. 4). These indicators are not validated against human maintainability judgements or established maintainability models — not reported.
    54	- Efficiency — input/output tokens, LLM call count, wall-clock LLM time, dollar cost from list prices [V] (p. 4).
    55	- Validation against human judgement (visual judge): 55 scenarios labelled with a blinded ranking interface — list-wise vs human strict Kendall τ = 0.716, top-1 accuracy 83.6%, top-2 overlap 80.4%, unrankable-set IoU 0.968; τ = 0.699 for page-existence and 0.731 for parent–child scenarios [V] (p. 13). Number and expertise of human raters and their agreement — not reported. Cross-judge: Claude Sonnet 4.5 on 139 scenarios from 5 apps gives inter-judge τ = 0.867 on the per-model ranking; no self-preference observed [V] (p. 13). Protocol smoke test (3 scenarios × 5 models): list-wise shuffle stability τ = 0.822, pair-wise position bias 23.3%, point-wise "ties-in-the-middle" [V] (pp. 12–13). Judge eligibility: Gemini 2.5 Pro and Claude Sonnet 4.5 ~100% anchor pass on a 33-scenario screening set; GPT-5.1 ~35% [V] (pp. 5, 13).
    56	- Navigation evaluator validity: Table 11 reports false positives of the automatic evaluator among flagged cases (6% page existence, 1% parent–child, 10% tab navigation) [V] (p. 16).
    57	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): Wilson 95% CIs for failure-mode proportions [V] (p. 8); ±1 SD error bars across apps in the cost plot [V] (p. 7). No significance tests for model differences; no run-to-run variance (single trial) [V] (pp. 6, 9).
    58	
    59	## 7. Key findings
    60	1. Build success is 100% for all six models; authors attribute this to the harness's verify-repair loop, not the model [V] (pp. 6–7, 12).
    61	2. NavPassRate: Opus 4.6 92%, GPT-5 89%, Haiku 4.5 85%, Gemini 2.5 Pro 82%, Gemini 2.5 Flash 62%, GPT-5 Mini 58% [V] (p. 7).
    62	3. Visual fidelity has not saturated: Borda 0.906 (Opus) to 0.130 (GPT-5 Mini); point-wise means 1.60–2.99/5, so even the best model stays below 3/5; Opus leads in 26 of 29 apps [V] (pp. 6–7). The gap is concentrated in cross-page Consistency: models re-implement navigation chrome inline per page instead of sharing a component [A] (p. 6).
    63	4. Maintainability is dissociated from visual fidelity: Opus writes 1,441 LoC (82 LoC/file) vs GPT-5 668 (33 LoC/file); GPT-5 has higher reuse (4.23 vs 3.83) and fewer dead components (7.8% vs 19.9%); ColorConsistency saturates at 0.74–0.85 [V] (pp. 6–7). Authors: "maintainability is uncorrelated with visual fidelity" [A] (p. 8) — no correlation coefficient is computed.
    64	5. Cost: $0.15 (GPT-5 Mini) to $2.90 (Opus) per app; GPT-5 ($0.50, Borda 0.542, NavPass 89%) dominates Haiku 4.5 and Gemini 2.5 Pro on cost and quality [V] (p. 7). Cheaper models fabricate content (Lorem ipsum, stock imagery) [A] (p. 7).
    65	6. Navigation failure taxonomy (n = 64 stratified hand-labelled failures from 3,486 executions): C1 blank starting page 7.8% [3.0, 18.3]; C2 route mapping error 10.9% [5.4, 20.9]; C3 target unreachable/occluded 32.8% [22.6, 45.0]; C4 click has no effect 48.4% [36.6, 60.4] [V] (p. 8). C4 (missing or mis-wired onClick) dominates for Opus and GPT-5 (75% of their labelled failures); C3 for GPT-5 Mini (67%); C1 for Gemini 2.5 Flash (42%) [V] (pp. 8, 15). Build checks do not catch silent event-handler bugs [A] (p. 8).
    66	7. Per-app difficulty varies widely: point-wise visual 3.62 (Notion) to 2.01 (Apple News); NavPass 0.45 (Medium) to 1.00 (Khan Academy) [V] (pp. 7, 12).
    67	
    68	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
    69	- Single trial per cell; multi-trial replication left to future work [A] (p. 9).
    70	- Visual scores come from Gemini 2.5 Pro, a competitor model class; mitigated by fixed judge, human calibration on 55 scenarios and a cross-judge check [A] (p. 9).
    71	- Web-rendering proxy: output is React + Tailwind, not native iOS/Android; native APIs not exercised [A] (p. 9).
    72	- Anchor-based judging depends on judges that follow the literal ranking instruction (GPT-5.1 fails) [A] (pp. 13–14).
    73	- Per-model failure proportions (n = 8–12) are "descriptive signatures rather than precise point estimates" [A] (p. 8).
    74	- Build success cannot discriminate models when a verify-repair loop is present [A] (p. 12).
    75	
    76	## 9. Limitations we identified
    77	- [I] Input is not screenshots alone: the agent also receives a human-reviewed page-relationship description (tab structure, parent–child triggers) (pp. 3, 6), although related work frames the benchmark as using "only screenshots" without "any structural prior" (p. 2). Results therefore describe reconstruction with an annotated navigation map, not pure black-box observation.
    78	- [I] Maintainability indicators are structural proxies (LoC, reuse, dead components, colour tokens) with no validation against developer judgement or standard metrics (complexity, duplication, smells, tests). LoC partly reflects how much content is reproduced, so "more LoC" is not clearly worse (p. 4, 7).
    79	- [I] "Uncorrelated"/"orthogonal" is asserted from six model means (p. 8); no correlation is computed at app or run level.
    80	- [I] Internal inconsistency in failure analysis: overall C4 = 48.4% (Table 4, p. 8), but the per-scenario-type projection (Table 11, p. 16) gives C4 of only 33% (parent–child) and 3% (tab navigation), which cannot average to 48.4% over the 581 interactive specs. The projection method or labels may differ; this needs clarification.
    81	- [I] Human validation of the visual judge: 55 scenarios with unreported number of raters, rater expertise and inter-rater agreement (p. 13); the protocol comparison uses only 3 scenarios × 5 models (p. 12).
    82	- [I] NavPass counts a pass when the content hash "changes meaningfully" for overlays (p. 5) — a lenient criterion; Table 11 shows 1–10% false positives in flagged cases (p. 16), but overall evaluator precision/recall on passes is not reported.
    83	- [I] Well-known apps chosen for "broad cultural recognition" (p. 3) are likely represented in model training data; contamination is not discussed.
    84	- [I] Single run per cell with stochastic agents; differences of a few NavPass points (e.g. Opus 92% vs GPT-5 89%) may be within run-to-run noise.
    85	- [I] Navigation evaluated only as page transitions; in-page behaviour, state, data and back-end logic are not tested.
    86	
    87	## 10. Threats to validity
    88	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): annotations drafted by an unnamed VLM, possibly from the same families evaluated; Gemini 2.5 Pro is both judge and candidate (self-preference check reported, p. 13); popular apps may be memorised [I].
    89	- External (generalisability of sample/context): 29 apps, 5–21 screens each; web proxy instead of native; one harness design; closed models only [I].
    90	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): NavPass measures routing, not full functional fidelity; Borda is relative (ordinal) and depends on the set of models compared; maintainability proxies unvalidated [I].
    91	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): single trial; no significance tests between models; Wilson CIs only for the failure sample (n = 64), per-model n = 8–12 [I].
    92	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): strong — benchmark, harness, evaluator and run artifacts released, one-command replay (pp. 9–10); decoding settings and drafting VLM not reported; closed models may change [I].
    93	
    94	## 11. Future research directions
    95	- Stated by authors [A]: multi-trial replication (p. 9); cross-platform/native extension (p. 9); stricter build gates (no `any`, strict null checks, lint) if compilation is to discriminate models (p. 12).
    96	- Suggested by us [I]: test pure screenshot-only input (without the page-relationship description) and interaction recordings as input; add in-page behavioural tests and data/state checks; validate maintainability proxies against developer ratings and standard static-analysis metrics; report run-to-run variance.
    97	
    98	## 12. Relevance to our research
    99	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ2, RQ3, RQ4, RQ5.
   100	- How it informs our work [I]: MobileForge is the closest existing design to our target study: it rebuilds whole multi-screen apps from screenshots of real, in-market apps with an agentic (vibe-coding-like) harness and scores functional navigation fidelity, visual fidelity and maintainability together. It shows these dimensions diverge (visual leader ≠ maintainability leader), giving direct support for joint evaluation. Its gaps — structural prior given as input, unvalidated maintainability proxies, single trials, no behaviour beyond navigation — are concrete design points for RQ5.
   101	
   102	## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
   103	| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
   104	|---|---|---|---|---|
   105	| RQ1 | Single-agent tool-using harness (8 tools, ≤50 iterations, tsc+vite repair loop) rebuilds React+TS+Tailwind projects from app screenshots plus a page-relationship description | p. 6 | V | moderate |
   106	| RQ2 | Navigation fidelity via 701 state-isolated Playwright tests: NavPass 58% (GPT-5 Mini) to 92% (Opus 4.6); build 100% for all | p. 7 | V | moderate |
   107	| RQ2 | Visual fidelity not saturated: point-wise means 1.60–2.99/5; Borda 0.13–0.91 | p. 6–7 | V | moderate |
   108	| RQ2 | Navigation failures: click has no effect 48.4%, target unreachable 32.8%, route error 10.9%, blank page 7.8% (n = 64, Wilson CIs) | p. 8 | V | weak |
   109	| RQ3 | Maintainability proxies (LoC, LoC/file, reuse, dead components, colour consistency): GPT-5 668 LoC, 7.8% dead vs Opus 1,441 LoC, 19.9% dead | p. 4, 7 | V | moderate |
   110	| RQ3 | Visual-fidelity leader is not maintainability leader; authors call them uncorrelated (no coefficient computed) | p. 6–8 | A | weak |
   111	| RQ4 | Anchor-referenced list-wise VLM judge vs human ranking on 55 scenarios: Kendall τ = 0.716, top-1 83.6%; cross-judge τ = 0.867 | p. 13 | V | moderate |
   112	| RQ4 | Pair-wise VLM judging shows 23.3% position bias; point-wise shows ties-in-the-middle (3-scenario smoke test) | p. 12–13 | V | weak |
   113	| RQ4 | Single trial per app–model cell; no significance tests between models | p. 6, 9 | V | moderate |
   114	| RQ4 | Build success saturates when a verify-repair loop is present and stops discriminating models | p. 12 | A | moderate |
   115	| RQ5 | Output is a web proxy, not native; agent also receives human-reviewed navigation description | p. 3, 9 | V | moderate |
   116	
   117	## 14. Key quotes
   118	> "Can a multimodal LLM read a folder of mobile-app screenshots and generate the source code for that app?" (p. 1)
   119	> "Build verification catches type errors but not silent event-handler bugs" (p. 8)
   120	> "Build success is a property of the harness, not the model." (p. 12)
   121	
   122	## Analyst notes
   123	- Reading coverage: whole PDF read (pp. 1–26), including appendices A–J; failure-gallery figures (pp. 18–26) seen only via captions; references skimmed.
   124	- Uncertainties: Table 4 vs Table 11 C4 shares do not reconcile; number of human raters for the 55-scenario alignment is not stated; the drafting VLM is not named. Peer-reviewed (EMNLP 2026 main, tier 1), very recent (Oct 2026), not yet replicated. The paper cites a concurrent submission by overlapping authors on interactive single-file webpages (p. 2) — unknown which paper.
